claim: Outer membrane proteins (OMPs) of gram-negative bacteria are synthesized in the cytosol and translocated across the inner membrane to reach the outer membrane.
source: OMPs are synthesized by cytosolic ribosomes, translocated across the inner membrane (IM), and finally delivered to the OM via the OMP biogenesis pathway (Rollauer et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rollauer et al., 2015

claim: SecYEG is a hetero-trimer composed of SecY, SecE, and SecG that is anchored to the inner membrane.
source: SecYEG, a hetero-trimer composed of the secretion channel SecY and two additional subunits SecE and SecG, is anchored to the IM and is responsible for moving most cell envelope proteins across the IM (Rapoport et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rapoport et al., 2017

claim: SecYEG is responsible for moving most cell envelope proteins across the inner membrane.
source: SecYEG, a hetero-trimer composed of the secretion channel SecY and two additional subunits SecE and SecG, is anchored to the IM and is responsible for moving most cell envelope proteins across the IM (Rapoport et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rapoport et al., 2017

claim: Periplasmic and outer membrane proteins enter the SecY channel via the SecA-dependent translocation pathway.
source: Periplasmic and OM proteins enter the channel in SecY via the SecA-dependent translocation pathway (Oswald et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Oswald et al., 2021

claim: SecA recognizes signal peptides on substrate proteins and powers them through the SecY channel using ATP hydrolysis.
source: They possess signal peptides recognized by SecA, which inserts a protein substrate into SecY and powers it through the channel using energy from ATP hydrolysis (Collinson, 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Collinson, 2019

claim: Type I signal peptidase (SPase I) cleaves the signal peptide to release the substrate from the inner membrane.
source: To release the substrate from the IM, a type I signal peptidase (SPase I) cleaves the signal peptide (Paetzel, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Paetzel, 2014

claim: OMPs are escorted by chaperones SurA or Skp toward BAM after signal peptide cleavage.
source: At this point, a periplasmic protein has reached its destination, but an OMP, escorted by the chaperones SurA or Skp, continues its journey toward BAM harbored in the OM (Sklar et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sklar et al., 2007

claim: BAM consists of five subunits, with BamA playing the major role in folding β-barrels and releasing matured products.
source: Five subunits constitute BAM, of which BamA plays the major role in folding a β-barrel and releasing the matured product (Tomasek and Kahne, 2021; Noinaj et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Tomasek and Kahne, 2021 and Noinaj et al., 2017

claim: The SecYEG translocon recruits additional proteins such as SecA, SecDF, YidC, and PpiD to form supercomplexes.
source: In Escherichia coli, the SecYEG translocon recruits additional proteins, such as SecA (Li et al., 2016), SecDF (Tsukazaki, 2018), YidC (Kumazaki et al., 2014), and PpiD (Antonoaea et al., 2008; Sachelaru et al., 2014), to form a variety of supercomplexes in different scenarios.
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: AF2Complex uses the iScore metric to evaluate the confidence of predicted protein-protein interactions.
source: For each pair of input proteins, AF2Complex predicts their structures simultaneously as a putative dimer and evaluates the interface score (iScore) of the resulting structural models to decide if they interact.
evidence: Describes the computational method used in the study

claim: iScore values range between 0 and 1, with interacting protein pairs typically returning positive iScores.
source: The value of iScore ranges between 0 and 1. Interacting protein pairs typically return a positive iScore, whereas non-interacting proteins usually return 0 or low iScores.
evidence: Describes the computational metric used in the study

claim: Minimum iScore thresholds of 0.40, 0.50, and 0.70 yield false positive rates of 1.2%, 0.4%, and <0.01%, respectively, based on benchmarks on ~7000 putatively non-interacting E. coli protein pairs.
source: According to previous benchmarks on a set of ~7000 putatively non-interacting protein pairs from E. coli, minimum iScore thresholds of 0.40, 0.50, and 0.70 yield false positive rates of 1.2, 0.4, and <0.01%, respectively (Gao et al., 2022b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Gao et al., 2022b describing benchmark results

claim: AF2Complex recalls 81%, 74%, and 34% of 440 heterodimeric complexes at iScore thresholds of 0.40, 0.50, and 0.70, respectively.
source: With respect to the capability of identifying and modeling true PPIs, on a set of 440 heterodimeric complexes whose experimental structures have been recently determined and were not used for AF2 model training, AF2Complex recalls 81, 74, and 34% of these benchmark targets at the same three iScore thresholds, respectively
evidence: Supported by citation to Gao et al., 2022b describing benchmark results

claim: PpiD and YfgM are predicted to interact with each other with iScores of ~0.73.
source: Reassuringly, these two proteins stand out at the very top of the predicted PPI rankings among the E. coli envelopome with iScores of ~0.73 in each case (Figure 1a, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Computational prediction result shown in Figure 1a

claim: PpiD interacts with SecY at the 12th rank with an iScore of 0.43.
source: Furthermore, PpiD hits SecY at the 12th rank (iScore = 0.43), corroborating previous experimental studies that SecY is an interacting partner of PpiD (Antonoaea et al., 2008; Sachelaru et al., 2014; Fürst et al., 2018).
evidence: Computational prediction corroborated by experimental citations

claim: Experimental evidence indicates that PpiD and YfgM belong to a super SecYEG translocon.
source: As a first test, we applied our PPI pipeline to the chaperones PpiD and YfgM because strong experimental evidence indicates that these two proteins belong to a super SecYEG translocon (Antonoaea et al., 2008; Sachelaru et al., 2014; Maddalo et al., 2011; Dartigalongue and Raina, 1998; Fürst et al., 2018; Jauss et al., 2019; Matern et al., 2010; Götzke et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental citations

claim: The predicted SecYEG/PpiD/YfgM supercomplex has an iScore of 0.73 and mean pLDDT of 79.
source: Subsequently, we modeled SecYEG together with PpiD and YfgM and acquired another very high confidence structure (iScore = 0.73, mean predicted local distance difference test [pLDDT] = 79, see Methods; Figure 1b–e).
evidence: Computational prediction result with confidence metrics

claim: PpiD has four domains in an open-arm shape plus an N-terminal transmembrane α-helix.
source: PpiD by itself has four domains in an open-arm shape, fitting its proposed chaperone role (Antonoaea et al., 2008; Matern et al., 2010), plus an N-terminal transmembrane α-helix (Figure 1b).
evidence: Structural prediction result shown in Figure 1b, consistent with experimental citations

claim: YfgM contains a tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domain that holds two α-helices of PpiD.
source: Within this domain, two α-helices (residues 167–189, 581–609) are held by the tetratricopeptide repeat (TPR) domain of YfgM, which inserts itself into the IM via a single hydrophobic α-helix.
evidence: Structural prediction result describing protein-protein interaction

claim: The PpiD/YfgM interface involves ~100 inter-protein residue-residue contacts including both hydrophobic and polar partners.
source: Their PPI interactions are quite extensive, including ~100 inter-protein residue-residue contacts involving both hydrophobic and polar partners (Figure 1b and c)
evidence: Structural analysis of predicted complex shown in Figure 1b and c

claim: The extensive PpiD/YfgM interactions may explain the strong binding affinity observed in experiments.
source: Their PPI interactions are quite extensive, including ~100 inter-protein residue-residue contacts involving both hydrophobic and polar partners (Figure 1b and c), which may explain the strong binding affinity observed in experiments (Maddalo et al., 2011).
evidence: Inference from structural prediction correlated with experimental observation

claim: SecY features a lateral gate embedded in the inner membrane that opens to release transmembrane segments including signal peptides.
source: In addition to the channel that connects the cytosol to the periplasm, SecY features a lateral gate embedded in the IM. It opens to release transmembrane segments, including the signal peptide of a substrate such as OmpA (Li et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Li et al., 2016

claim: In vivo photo cross-linking studies found numerous sites at the SecY lateral gate probed by PpiD.
source: In vivo photo cross-linking studies found numerous sites at the lateral gate probed by PpiD (Sachelaru et al., 2014; Jauss et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by experimental citations

claim: The predicted structure reveals that PpiD guards the lateral gate of SecY with its α-helix.
source: Indeed, our structure reveals that PpiD guards the lateral gate of SecY with its α-helix (Figure 1b and d), which occupies the same position as a signal peptide leaving the SecY gate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Structural prediction result shown in Figure 1b and d

claim: The PpiD α-helix occupies the same position as a signal peptide leaving the SecY gate.
source: Indeed, our structure reveals that PpiD guards the lateral gate of SecY with its α-helix (Figure 1b and d), which occupies the same position as a signal peptide leaving the SecY gate (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: The Cα RMSD of SecY between the predicted structure and an X-ray crystal structure co-crystallized with an OmpA signal peptide is 2.4 Å.
source: In superposition with a SecY crystal structure co-crystallized with an OmpA signal peptide, the Cα RMSD of SecY is 2.4 Å between the X-ray and computed structures.
evidence: Structural comparison metric between predicted and experimental structures

claim: SecY in the predicted model is in an open conformation to accommodate the α-helix of PpiD.
source: Thus, SecY in our model is open to accommodate the α-helix of PpiD, in comparison to an electron microscopy (EM) structure of E. coli SecY in which the gate is closed (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Structural comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1

claim: Five SecY residues (Ile91, Leu94, Leu127, Phe130, and Phe286) that show strong cross-linking signals make direct physical contacts (<4.5 Å) with PpiD in the predicted structure.
source: For example, strong cross-linking signals have been found for five SecY residues (Sachelaru et al., 2014; Jauss et al., 2019), Ile91SecY, Leu94SecY, Leu127SecY, Phe130SecY, and Phe286SecY, and all make direct physical contacts (<4.5 Å) with PpiD in our structural model (Figure 1d).
evidence: Predicted structure explains experimental cross-linking data, shown in Figure 1d

claim: Direct contacts exist between a hydrophobic pocket of PpiD and SecG, explaining the experimentally observed crosslinking of Phe122PpiD to SecG.
source: Moreover, we identified direct contacts between a hydrophobic pocket of PpiD and SecG, explaining the experimentally observed crosslinking of Phe122PpiD to SecG (Fürst et al., 2018; Figure 1e).
evidence: Predicted structure explains experimental cross-linking data, shown in Figure 1e

claim: The predicted structure assigns SecG a functional role in coordinating with PpiD.
source: The interaction assigns SecG a functional role in coordinating with PpiD.
evidence: Inference from predicted structural interactions

claim: DsbA is ranked third among PPI partners of PpiD with a high confidence iScore of 0.55.
source: Among the top hits for PPI partners of PpiD, a fascinating discovery is DsbA, ranked third with a high confidence iScore of 0.55.
evidence: Computational prediction result

claim: DsbA donates its disulfide bond to substrates and is critical to the folding of nascent proteins leaving the SecY channel.
source: DsbA donates its disulfide bond to a substrate in need; thus, it is critical to the folding of a nascent protein as it leaves the SecY channel (Kadokura and Beckwith, 2009; Goemans et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kadokura and Beckwith, 2009 and Goemans et al., 2014

claim: The predicted SecYEG/PpiD/YfgM/DsbA supercomplex has an iScore of 0.71 and mean pLDDT of 78.
source: In a predicted structure of this supercomplex (iScore = 0.71, mean pLDDT = 78, Figure 2a)
evidence: Computational prediction result with confidence metrics

claim: PpiD uses its parvulin-like domain to grip DsbA in the predicted structure.
source: In a predicted structure of this supercomplex (iScore = 0.71, mean pLDDT = 78, Figure 2a), PpiD uses its 'hand' to grip DsbA, as observed in the top model of the pair because their interactions do not interfere with other members of the translocon. The hand of PpiD is a parvulin-like domain
evidence: Structural prediction result shown in Figure 2a

claim: The parvulin-like domain of PpiD lacks peptidyl-prolyl isomerase (PPIase) activity due to mutation of a critical histidine.
source: The hand of PpiD is a parvulin-like domain, but it is devoid of the peptidyl-prolyl isomerase (PPIase) activity canonical to parvulin, due to the mutation of a critical histidine (Weininger et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weininger et al., 2010

claim: The catalytically inactive PPIase pocket of PpiD is hydrophobic and buries the aromatic sidechain of Phe148DsbA.
source: As our structure reveals, the catalytically inactive pocket of the PPIase domain is hydrophobic and buries the aromatic sidechain of Phe148DsbA, which becomes a hot-spot residue surrounded by six hydrophobic residues of PpiD upon complexation (Figure 2b).
evidence: Structural prediction result shown in Figure 2b

claim: Three pairs of salt-bridges are formed around the hydrophobic contacts between PpiD and DsbA.
source: In addition, three pairs of salt-bridges are formed around the hydrophobic contacts, contributing to specific recognition.
evidence: Structural prediction result describing protein-protein interactions

claim: The catalytic cysteines of DsbA (Cys49 and Cys52) are on the opposite side to the PpiD-DsbA interface and are open to engage a substrate.
source: Notably, the catalytic cysteines of DsbA, Cys49DsbA and Cys52DsbA, are on the opposite side to the protein-protein interface (Figure 2a); thus, they are open to engage a substrate as it emerges from the SecY channel.
evidence: Structural prediction result shown in Figure 2a

claim: DsbA resides on PpiD transiently to improve its chance of encountering a substrate.
source: Based on this model, we hypothesize that DsbA resides on PpiD transiently to improve its chance of encountering a substrate.
evidence: Hypothesis based on predicted structure

claim: Polypeptide translocation triggers the dissociation of PpiD from SecY.
source: Polypeptide translocation triggers the dissociation of PpiD from SecY (Sachelaru et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sachelaru et al., 2014

claim: PpiD dissociation from SecY is realized by a substrate pushing out of the SecY gate and repelling the PpiD helix bound to the gate.
source: The modeled complex suggests that PpiD dissociation is realized by pushing a substrate out of the SecY gate, e.g., the signal peptide, which then repels the PpiD helix bound to the gate.
evidence: Mechanistic hypothesis based on predicted structure

claim: LepB is the peptidase that removes signal peptides from OMPs in E. coli.
source: For an OMP, a key next step is the removal of the signal peptide by the peptidase LepB in E. coli (Paetzel, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Paetzel, 2014

claim: The predicted LepB/PpiD/YfgM/proOmpA complex has an iScore of 0.64 and mean pLDDT of 80.
source: We generated a structural model of LepB in complex with a precursor OmpA (proOmpA) chain (residue 1–87) grasped by PpiD (iScore = 0.64, mean pLDDT = 80; Figure 3).
evidence: Computational prediction result with confidence metrics

claim: The OmpA cleavage site Ala21 directly contacts the LepB active site triad (Ser89, Ser91, and Lys146) at ~4 Å distance in the predicted structure.
source: The OmpA cleavage site, Ala21OmpA, directly contacts the LepB active site triad, Ser89LepB, Ser91LepB, and Lys146LepB at ~4 Å away from the alanine.
evidence: Structural prediction result describing active site positioning

claim: In the predicted model, proOmpA contributes a β-strand to form a parallel β-sheet with LepB.
source: In our model, the proOmpA chain contributes a β-strand to form a parallel β-sheet with LepB, as has been speculated (Paetzel, 2014).
evidence: Structural prediction result consistent with speculation from Paetzel, 2014

claim: A crystal structure of SurA exhibits three domains: a core domain (split into N- and C-terminal subdomains) and two PPIase domains, P1 and P2.
source: A crystal structure of SurA exhibits three domains: a core domain (split into N- and C-terminal subdomains) and two PPIase domains, P1 and P2 (Bitto and McKay, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bitto and McKay, 2002

claim: P2 of SurA retains PPIase activity but P1 does not.
source: P2 retains PPIase activity but P1 does not (Behrens et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Behrens et al., 2001

claim: A crystal structure of SurA shows P1 packing with the core domain forming a cradle-like closed conformation.
source: In this crystal structure, P1 further packs with the core domain forming a cradle-like structure (Bitto and McKay, 2002), referred to as the closed conformation of SurA.
evidence: Supported by citation to Bitto and McKay, 2002

claim: A crystal structure of the SurA homodimer lacking P2s displays an open conformation where two P1s hold a dodecapeptide at the dimeric interface.
source: By contrast, another crystal structure of the SurA homodimer lacking P2s displays an open conformation, where two P1s are uncoupled from the core domains to hold a dodecapeptide at the dimeric interface between P1s (Xu et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xu et al., 2007

claim: AF2Complex predicted two major conformations for full-length SurA: one closed conformation resembling the crystal structure and one open conformation.
source: To explore conformations of SurA, we predicted structures for a single, full-length SurA and obtain two major conformations (Figure 4a). One conformation closely resembles the cradle-like closed conformation with a backbone Cα RMSD of 2.4 Å from the crystal structure. The other mimics the open conformation but incorporates P2 absent in the X-ray structure.
evidence: Computational prediction result shown in Figure 4a

claim: The predicted closed conformation of SurA has a backbone Cα RMSD of 2.4 Å from the crystal structure.
source: One conformation closely resembles the cradle-like closed conformation with a backbone Cα RMSD of 2.4 Å from the crystal structure.
evidence: Structural comparison metric between predicted and experimental structures

claim: The predicted open conformation of SurA resembles a 'three-prong hook' where both P1 and P2 swing away from their resting position in the closed conformation.
source: Overall, the open conformation resembles a 'three-prong hook,' where both P1 and P2 swing away from their resting position in the closed conformation.
evidence: Description of predicted structure

claim: In the presence of SurA, the periplasmic domain of OmpA maintains its native-like fold while the β-barrel region completely unravels and wraps around SurA.
source: In the presence of SurA, the periplasmic domain maintains the same fold, but remarkably, the non-native β-barrel region completely unravels and wraps around SurA (Figure 4b–c).
evidence: Structural prediction result shown in Figure 4b-c

claim: The predicted unfolded OmpA substrate wrapping around SurA is consistent with small angle neutron scattering data suggesting an expanded and unfolded OmpA substrate.
source: This is consistent with small angle neutron scattering data that suggests an expanded and unfolded OmpA substrate (Marx et al., 2020).
evidence: Predicted structure consistent with experimental data from Marx et al., 2020

claim: The SurA/OmpA dimer is not stable with very low iScores of ~0.05, reflecting uncertainty due to many possible conformations.
source: The SurA/OmpA dimer is not stable as different wrapping configurations were observed in two separate structure models, leading to very low iScores of ~0.05, reflecting uncertainty due to the possibility of many conformations.
evidence: Computational prediction result with low confidence score

claim: In both predicted SurA/OmpA structures, the OmpA polypeptide passes through a crevice at the SurA core domain where Tyr126 consistently attracts a substrate aromatic residue with π-π interactions.
source: Nevertheless, the SurA/OmpA models appear physical and provide a hypothetical basis for how the chaperone SurA could prevent a polypeptide chain from aggregating and present an unfolded polypeptide to BAM for its final assembly. Intriguingly, in both predicted complex structures, the OmpA polypeptide passes through a SurA crevice at its core domain, where Tyr126SurA consistently attracts a substrate aromatic residue with π-π interactions.
evidence: Structural prediction result describing consistent interaction

claim: SurA may recognize OMPs through Tyr126 attracting aromatic residues, which are enriched in OMPs.
source: This may be one mechanism by which SurA recognizes OMPs, which are enriched with aromatic residues (Xu et al., 2007; Hennecke et al., 2005).
evidence: Hypothesis based on predicted structure and literature about OMP composition

claim: The disordered β-barrel region of OmpA has few interactions with SurA, which could explain how the system avoids high-energy expenditure for β-barrel release.
source: Moreover, the disordered β-barrel region has few interactions with SurA could explain how the system avoids high-energy expenditure for β-barrel release.
evidence: Inference from predicted structural interactions

claim: Two key β-signal residues (Y189 and F191) of OmpA do not make direct physical contact with SurA in both predicted models.
source: Of note, two key 'β-signal' residues (Tommassen, 2010), Y189 and F191 of OmpA, do not make direct physical contact with SurA in both models.
evidence: Structural prediction result describing absence of specific interactions

claim: SurA recognizes itself in envelopome screening at a high confidence iScore of 0.53.
source: Interestingly, SurA recognizes itself at a high confidence iScore of 0.53 (Figure 4d).
evidence: Computational prediction result shown in Figure 4d

claim: The top model of a SurA homodimer exhibits twofold rotational symmetry with swapped P1 domains, leading to an open conformation different from the monomeric open conformation.
source: The top model of a SurA homodimer exhibits twofold rotational symmetry, in which P1 domains are swapped, leading to an open conformation quite different from the above one (Figure 4e–f).
evidence: Structural prediction result shown in Figure 4e-f

claim: The dimeric SurA conformation resembles a four-prong hook and provides another configuration to handle potentially large clients.
source: This conformation, like a four-prong hook, provides SurA with another configuration to handle clients, potentially large ones, consistent with experimental conclusions (Li et al., 2018; Calabrese et al., 2020).
evidence: Structural prediction result consistent with experimental conclusions

claim: SurA functions mainly as a monomer but may act as a dimer for a large client.
source: SurA functions mainly as a monomer but may act as a dimer for a large client (Li et al., 2018; Calabrese et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2018 and Calabrese et al., 2020

claim: Envelopome screening confidently detected that SurA interacts with BamA.
source: Excitingly, envelopome screening also confidently detected that SurA interacts with BamA, the anchoring subunit of BAM at the final stop of OMPs.
evidence: Computational prediction result

claim: The predicted BAM/SurA supercomplex has an iScore of 0.75 and mean pLDDT of 84.
source: To understand how SurA interacts with BAM, we subsequently used AF2Complex to probe potential interactions of SurA with all five BAM constituents (BamABCDE) and acquired a high confidence complex structure (iScore = 0.75, mean pLDDT = 84; Figure 5a–b).
evidence: Computational prediction result with confidence metrics

claim: The predicted BAM structure closely mimics a known crystal structure of the complex determined at 2.9 Å resolution (PDB 5D0O).
source: Because BAM has been extensively studied structurally (Tomasek and Kahne, 2021; Wu et al., 2020), we focus on describing its interaction with SurA, though the predicted BAM structure closely mimics a known crystal structure of the complex determined at 2.9 Å resolution (PDB 5D0O; Gu et al., 2016).
evidence: Structural comparison with experimental structure from Gu et al., 2016

claim: The alignment of the predicted BAM structure with the crystal structure yields a very high TM-score of 0.94.
source: The alignment of the two complex structures yielding a very high TM-score of 0.94.
evidence: Structural comparison metric between predicted and experimental structures

claim: SurA mainly interacts with BamA in the N-terminal domains of both proteins.
source: Overall, SurA mainly interacts with BamA, with similar interactions observed in both the top supercomplex and the BamA/SurA dimer structures, in the N-terminal domains of both proteins (Figure 5b–c).
evidence: Structural prediction result shown in Figure 5b-c

claim: Residues Gln23 to Val28 of SurA form a β-sheet with the β2 strand of POTRA1 (the N-terminal domain of BamA) in the predicted structure.
source: Gln23SurA to Val28SurA, largely missing in the crystal structures of SurA (Bitto and McKay, 2002; Xu et al., 2007), now form a β-sheet with the β2 strand of POTRA1, the N-terminal domain of BamA.
evidence: Structural prediction result describing specific interaction

claim: Asp26 of SurA is located at the center of the SurA/BamA interface, explaining why it is cross-linked to BamA.
source: The structure explains the result that Asp26SurA is cross-linked to BamA (Wang et al., 2016) because Asp26SurA is located at the center of the SurA/BamA interface.
evidence: Predicted structure explains experimental cross-linking data from Wang et al., 2016

claim: SurA adopts a closed conformation in the BAM/SurA complex, but the P2 domain rotates ~45° from its crystal position to engage additional contacts with BamA and BamE.
source: Furthermore, SurA adopts a closed conformation in our model, but the P2 domain rotates ~45° from its crystal position (Bitto and McKay, 2002) to engage additional contacts with BamA and BamE (Figure 5d–e).
evidence: Structural prediction result shown in Figure 5d-e

claim: Asn336 of SurA forms a hydrogen bond with the backbone oxygen atom of Gly275 of BamA in the predicted structure.
source: For example, Asn336SurA forms a hydrogen bond with the backbone oxygen atom of Gly275BamA; in the same cross-linking study (Wang et al., 2016), Asn336SurA is implied to interact with BamA.
evidence: Predicted structure consistent with cross-linking data from Wang et al., 2016

claim: SurA and BamA initiate payload transfer via specific docking at their N-terminal domains.
source: These results invite a hypothesis that SurA and BamA initiate payload transfer via specific docking at their N-terminal domains.
evidence: Hypothesis based on predicted structural interactions

claim: BepA ranked third among BamA PPI screening hits with high confidence.
source: SurA led us to BamA, for which we conducted another envelopome PPI screening. The top six hits include all expected ones, the other four BAM factors and SurA, but unexpectedly, BepA ranked third with high confidence (Figure 6a–b).
evidence: Computational prediction result shown in Figure 6a-b

claim: BepA cleans up stalled OMP folding at BAM.
source: However, a literature search quickly revealed that BepA is highly relevant because it cleans up stalled OMP folding at BAM (Narita et al., 2013; Soltes et al., 2017)
evidence: Supported by citations to Narita et al., 2013 and Soltes et al., 2017

claim: Interactions between BepA and BAM have been documented experimentally.
source: and its interactions with BAM have been documented (Narita et al., 2013; Daimon et al., 2017), though no structure of the complex is available.
evidence: Supported by citations to Narita et al., 2013 and Daimon et al., 2017

claim: The predicted BepA/BAM supercomplex has an iScore of 0.68 and mean pLDDT of 85.
source: Consequently, we modeled BepA and the full BAM complex altogether, obtaining a high confidence model (iScore = 0.68, mean pLDDT = 85, Figure 6c).
evidence: Computational prediction result with confidence metrics

claim: The BepA/BamA interfaces are quite similar (interface Cα RMSD 1.2 Å) between the dimer and the supercomplex structure.
source: Overall, the BepA/BamA interfaces are quite similar (interface Cα RMSD 1.2 Å) between the dimer and the supercomplex structure.
evidence: Structural comparison metric between different predicted structures

claim: Extensive contacts are present between all five periplasmic domains (POTRA1−5) of BamA and the two domains (protease and TPR) of BepA.
source: Extensive contacts are present between all five periplasmic domains (POTRA1−5) of BamA and the two domains (protease and TPR) of BepA.
evidence: Structural prediction result describing protein-protein interactions

claim: BepA/BamA contacts can be clustered into two main groups: between POTRA1 and TPR, and between POTRA3-4 and the protease domains.
source: They can be clustered into two main groups scattered between the POTRA1 and TPR and between POTRA3-4 and the protease domains (Figure 6d).
evidence: Structural prediction result shown in Figure 6d

claim: Phe404 of BepA has been observed to have strong photo cross-linking signals to BamA.
source: Strong photo cross-linking signals to BamA have been observed previously for several residues of TPR including Phe404BepA (Narita et al., 2013; Daimon et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by experimental citations

claim: Phe404 of BepA belongs to the first interaction cluster with five BamA residues, particularly Pro47, in the predicted structure.
source: According to our model, Phe404BepA belongs to the first interaction cluster with five BamA residues, particularly Pro47BamA.
evidence: Predicted structure explains experimental cross-linking data

claim: Gln428 of BepA is cross-linked to BamA and establishes a specific hydrogen bond with Arg49 of BamA in the predicted model.
source: Another residue cross-linked to BamA is Gln428BepA, which establishes a specific hydrogen bond with Arg49BamA in our model.
evidence: Predicted structure explains experimental cross-linking data

claim: A segment (residue 154–192) of the BepA metalloprotease domain, termed an 'active-site lid', is absent in crystal structures of BepA alone, presumably due to its flexibility.
source: Crystal structures of BepA alone have been solved, but a segment (residue 154–192) of the metalloprotease domain is absent in these structures, presumably due to its flexibility (Daimon et al., 2017; Bryant et al., 2020; Shahrizal et al., 2019; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental citations

claim: The active-site lid of BepA was speculated to be important to protease function because its movement could expose (open state) or cover (closed state) the catalytic site.
source: The segment, termed an 'active-site lid,', was speculated to be important to the protease function of BepA because its movement could either expose (open state) or cover (closed state) the catalytic site, the HEXXH motif (Bryant et al., 2020).
